questions.q: What is the key difference between a plain chatbot and an AI agent?
options: An agent can only answer in a single language
An agent can take real actions, such as calling tools, not just produce text
A chatbot always runs faster than an agent
There is no meaningful difference between them
questions.explanation: A chatbot only replies with text. An agent connects a language model to real tools, letting it take actions like reading files, sending emails, or calling other agents.

questions.q: Why do companies build multi-agent systems instead of one large agent?
options: Specialization, scalability, and safer separation of duties
It reduces the total number of trust boundaries to zero
A single agent cannot legally be deployed
Multi-agent systems require no orchestration at all
questions.explanation: Specialized agents tend to perform better, individual agents can be upgraded independently, and giving each agent only the access it needs is inherently safer.

questions.q: What is a 'trust boundary' in a multi-agent system?
options: The maximum number of agents allowed in a system
A firewall rule blocking external traffic
The invisible line crossed whenever two agents communicate with each other
The physical server hosting all the agents
questions.explanation: Every time two agents exchange a message, a trust boundary is crossed. If that boundary isn't protected, an attacker can inject, intercept, or impersonate along it.

questions.q: What does the A2A protocol primarily standardize?
options: How agents describe themselves, get discovered, and exchange task messages
The programming language agents must be written in
The physical hardware agents must run on
How many agents a company is allowed to deploy
questions.explanation: A2A defines a shared standard so agents built by different companies can discover each other, format task messages consistently, and return results in a common format.

questions.q: Where is an Agent Card typically served from?
options: A random port chosen at runtime
A private database only the orchestrator can query
An encrypted file sent via email
A fixed, predictable path: /.well-known/agent.json
questions.explanation: Every A2A agent publishes its Agent Card at the standard, predictable path /.well-known/agent.json, making it easy for both legitimate orchestrators and attackers to find.

questions.q: Which coordination pattern creates a single point of failure, where compromising one central component means controlling the entire system?
options: Peer-to-Peer (mesh) pattern
Pipeline (chain) pattern
Orchestrator (hub-and-spoke) pattern
Hierarchical (tree) pattern
questions.explanation: In the Orchestrator/hub-and-spoke pattern, a central agent controls all task distribution. Compromising it gives an attacker control over the whole system.

questions.q: In the peer-to-peer (mesh) coordination pattern, what is the main weakness?
options: Trust propagation, where one compromised agent can poison all its peers
It requires a single central orchestrator to function
It cannot support more than two agents
It has no communication between agents at all
questions.explanation: Since agents in a mesh talk directly to each other with no central authority, a compromised agent can spread poisoned data or fake trust to all its peers.

questions.q: What is 'capability jumping' in a pipeline (chain) coordination pattern?
options: Agents gaining new skills automatically over time
A malicious payload injected at an early, low-privilege stage surviving to execute at a later, high-privilege stage
The pipeline randomly skipping stages for performance
Two agents swapping their roles mid-task
questions.explanation: Since each agent's output becomes the next agent's input, a payload planted early in the chain can ride along undetected until it reaches a stage with more power.

questions.q: Why is LLM-driven orchestration considered risky?
options: It uses more electricity than rule-based orchestration
It cannot process JSON data
Since the orchestrator decides actions based on natural language, that same language can be used to manipulate its decisions
It only works with a single agent at a time
questions.explanation: When an LLM decides the workflow using natural language, that workflow becomes attackable using natural language too, since words effectively become control commands.

questions.q: What does an empty 'security' field in an Agent Card typically indicate?
options: The agent has the strongest possible security
The card is corrupted and cannot be read
No authentication is required to interact with that agent, a red flag
The agent has been deprecated and removed
questions.explanation: An empty security field means no authentication scheme is defined for the agent, signaling that anyone who finds it can potentially call it directly.

questions.q: What is the core idea behind Agent Card spoofing?
options: Publishing a fake card that copies a real agent's name and skills but points the URL to an attacker-controlled server
Deleting a legitimate agent's card from the registry
Encrypting an Agent Card so no one can read it
Changing an agent's name to something unrelated
questions.explanation: Since cards are usually unsigned, an attacker can copy a real agent's identity and skills while redirecting the URL field to their own server, silently intercepting traffic.

questions.q: Why does the 'incremental trust' technique (hiding a bypass in conversation history) evade detection better than a direct request?
options: It uses a different network protocol entirely
It disables the LLM's ability to read text
The malicious signal sits in history rather than the main prompt, and is phrased in calm, business-like language scanners don't flag
It requires the attacker to have admin credentials
questions.explanation: Many detection tools only scan the current prompt for obvious keywords. Placing the bypass instruction in history, phrased like a normal business note, avoids those triggers entirely.

questions.q: Why is history injection so effective against LLM-based agents?
options: It requires admin access to the orchestrator
The LLM treats all conversation history as trusted, and scanners usually check only the current prompt
It disables the agent's network connection
It encrypts the attacker's payload so it cannot be read
questions.explanation: An LLM cannot distinguish real history from attacker-supplied history, and most detection tools inspect only the current prompt, so malicious instructions hidden in history slip through.

questions.q: After a workflow-integrity bypass attempt, which two response fields confirm whether the security scan was actually skipped?
options: http_status and content_length
server_name and timestamp
steps_completed and security_report
user_id and session_token
questions.explanation: If security_scan is missing from steps_completed, or security_report returns null, that confirms the mandatory scan step was skipped entirely.

questions.q: In a rogue agent registration attack, why does the victim usually notice nothing wrong?
options: The attack only runs at night
The rogue agent forwards requests to the real agent, so a valid response is still returned
The orchestrator stops working entirely
The rogue agent deletes all logs on the orchestrator
questions.explanation: The intercept-and-forward pattern logs the data but still forwards the request to the real agent, so the victim receives a correct answer and suspects nothing.

questions.q: Which evasion technique involves adding a random delay to a rogue agent's responses?
options: Capability subset
Timing mimicry (jitter)
Selective interception
Registration timing
questions.explanation: Jitter adds a small random delay so the rogue agent's response time matches the real agent's latency profile, since instant replies can look robotic and suspicious.

questions.q: What is the 'confused deputy' problem in multi-agent systems?
options: An agent forgetting its own configuration
Two agents arguing over which one should run first
A trusted component being tricked into handing valuable data or access to the wrong party
An agent that has no tools assigned to it
questions.explanation: The confused deputy pattern describes a trusted component, like an orchestrator, being manipulated into granting access or data to an attacker instead of the legitimate party.

questions.q: What is the correct defense against workflow integrity attacks that skip a security scan?
options: Only run the scan when the user requests it
Remove the security agent entirely
Ask the LLM more politely to run the scan
Hard-code the security scan as a mandatory step in fixed code, outside the LLM's control
questions.explanation: If the LLM can decide whether a security step runs, a prompt can talk it out of running. Enforcing the step in fixed code means no prompt, however clever, can skip it.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Agent Card spoofing is so easy in default A2A systems?
options: Agent Cards require a password to read
Agent Cards are stored in a hidden database
Agent Cards are encrypted end-to-end
Agent Cards are, by default, not cryptographically signed, so a forged card cannot be detected
questions.explanation: By default, A2A Agent Cards are unsigned. Without a signature, nothing proves a card is genuine, so an attacker can forge one or tamper with the URL field undetected.

questions.q: According to the module's three-question mental model, what should you ask about any multi-agent system?
options: How fast is it, how much does it cost, and how big is it?
Who is talking, what are they allowed to do, and can I trust what they said?
What language is it written in, who deployed it, and when was it built?
How many agents exist, what is their uptime, and who pays for hosting?
questions.explanation: These three questions map directly to identity verification, authorization/least privilege, and message integrity, the three pillars that most multi-agent attacks exploit when left unanswered.
